title: He Scored 19,346 Runs for New Zealand. On Friday, Kane Williamson Said Goodbye.
excerpt: The Fab Four's quietest genius retires from international cricket at 35 — 485 runs short of 10,000 in Tests — with Virat Kohli leading tributes to a rival who became a brother.
body:
Kane Williamson announced his immediate retirement from international cricket on Friday, ending a 16-year career that made him New Zealand's greatest run-scorer and one of the most respected batsmen of his generation. He will not play in the second Test against England at The Oval, choosing instead to walk away mid-series — a rare decision that underlined the finality of his choice.

"I've always felt a strong drive and hunger for international cricket, and I take pride in knowing I've given it my all in every match I've played for New Zealand," Williamson said in a statement released by New Zealand Cricket. "Continuing with anything less wouldn't be right and I feel fortunate to step away on my own terms."

He leaves behind staggering numbers: 110 Tests, 9,515 runs at an average of 54.06, with 33 centuries and six double hundreds. Across all formats, he amassed 19,346 runs in 378 internationals — more than any New Zealander in history. He captained the Black Caps in 40 Tests, winning 22, and led them to the inaugural World Test Championship title in 2021.

## The Kohli Bond

Within hours of the announcement, Virat Kohli posted an emotional tribute on X that captured what Williamson meant to an entire generation of cricket. The two first met as teenagers at the 2008 Under-19 World Cup in Malaysia, where Kohli captained India to the title.

"From an opponent to a friend over the years," Kohli wrote. "It's been a pleasure watching you bat and compete against you over so many years, but more than that, I value our friendship and shared perspectives on the game and beyond. I continue to cherish every time we speak or meet. Wishing you nothing but the best always, brother. You've done your bit, you deserve to enjoy all of it now and put your feet up. Well done mate, life's only just begun."

The message was vintage Kohli — direct, affectionate, and unmistakably genuine. ICC Chairman Jay Shah also congratulated Williamson, calling his career "built on class, humility, and outstanding leadership."

## The Last of the Fab Four

Williamson's retirement means all four members of cricket's celebrated "Fab Four" — Williamson, Kohli, Steve Smith, and Joe Root — have now either retired from at least one format or are winding down. Of the quartet, Williamson was the quietest and perhaps the most technically complete. While Kohli had the intensity, Smith the eccentricity, and Root the volume of runs, Williamson played with a stillness that made batting look like a meditative act.

He averaged 69.7 in home Tests — second only to Don Bradman among batsmen with significant careers. He held the record for the fewest innings to 32 Test centuries (172), beating Smith, Ponting, and Tendulkar. He scored five centuries in the fourth innings of Tests, a joint record with Younis Khan.

Yet he left 485 runs short of 10,000 in Tests, a milestone that seemed inevitable when the series began at Lord's. His final Test innings produced just 0 and 18 as England won comfortably. Williamson chose peace over milestones.

## An IPL Favourite

For Indian fans, Williamson was more than an opponent. He was an IPL regular, spending the bulk of his franchise career at Sunrisers Hyderabad, where he became captain and scored 2,128 runs in 78 matches at a strike rate above 125. Hyderabad embraced him — his calm leadership and matchday awareness made him a crowd favourite at the Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium, even though the franchise never won another title under his watch.

His most memorable IPL knock may have been his unbeaten 89 off 51 balls against Delhi Capitals in 2022, when he almost single-handedly dragged SRH into the playoffs. Indian fans who watched him demolish spin on subcontinental pitches knew they were watching something special — a batsman who understood Indian conditions better than most visiting players ever would.

## The WTC Final That Changed Everything

The defining moment of Williamson's career, for Indian cricket fans, remains the World Test Championship final at the Ageas Bowl in Southampton in June 2021. New Zealand beat India by eight wickets in a match that was spread over six days because of rain. Williamson scored 49 in the second innings, shepherding the chase with the composure that defined his career.

For India, it was a painful loss — the culmination of two years of dominant Test cricket that ended in defeat. For Williamson, it was vindication: a team long considered too small to compete on the biggest stage had just won Test cricket's ultimate prize.

## What the Diaspora Loses

NRI cricket fans in the US, UK, and Canada have a complicated relationship with rival captains. They cheer for India, but they respect greatness. Williamson was the opponent you could never dislike — the batsman who never sledged, never postured, and never needed to. His departure marks the slow closing of an era that coincided with the peak years of Indian cricket fandom abroad, when the Fab Four made every bilateral series feel like an event.

He will continue playing franchise cricket — currently with Middlesex in England's T20 Blast — but international cricket will be poorer for his absence. The Black Caps will need to rebuild around younger talent, and the second Test at The Oval will feel different without the man who made batting look effortless.

As Kohli put it: life's only just begun.
